endorsements.quote: In tumor staging, AI can serve as an assistive tool but should not replace comprehensive clinical judgment in the absence of sufficient prospective evidence.

AI models intended for prognostic assessment should undergo external validation across centers, imaging devices, patient populations, and clinically relevant subgroups prior to clinical adoption, with attention to potential performance disparities.
Before entering routine clinical practice, AI tools should be evaluated through prospective studies or real-world evidence to verify their actual clinical value.

Dynamic regulatory and quality control mechanisms should be established to monitor safety and stability over time, data shift, performance drift, and performance in relevant patient subgroups after deployment.
Once clinically significant performance degradation is identified, standardized protocols shall govern model recalibration, retraining, temporary suspension, or clinical decommissioning.
The scope of application, target populations, and limitations of AI models should be clearly defined to avoid inappropriate generalization or misuse.

AI models used for oncologic imaging diagnosis should provide interpretable outputs sufficient to support clinical understanding of model focus, decision rationale, potential failure modes, and human expert review or override when clinically appropriate.

AI models intended for prognostic assessment should undergo external validation across centers, imaging devices, patient populations, and clinically relevant subgroups prior to clinical adoption, with attention to potential performance disparities.
AI models used in surgical navigation or intelligent surgical assistance systems should undergo thorough validation of safety, accuracy, and stability prior to clinical deployment.

unlisted_practices: Train physicians before clinical deployment to understand the capabilities, limitations, and risks of AI tools.
Integrate AI tools deeply with clinical information systems such as PACS and RIS to enable actionable clinical workflows.
Use privacy-preserving collaborative modeling techniques in multicenter collaborations to avoid direct sharing of raw imaging data.
Evaluate the impact of privacy-preserving techniques on image quality and model performance to avoid degrading diagnostic capability.
Harmonize imaging acquisition parameters and preprocessing pipelines to mitigate inter-institutional variability.
Use automated or semi-automated annotation and segmentation combined with expert review to improve consistency and reproducibility.
Use AI in radiotherapy segmentation only under professional supervision.
Lightweight AI tools may be preferentially deployed in primary or resource-limited settings to improve accessibility.
